JUDGMENT
P. Kumararatnam, J.
The above-named Accused-Appellant (hereinafter after referred to as the
Appellant) was indicted by the Director General of Bribery Commission in
the High Court of the Western Province holden in Colombo on the following
charges:
1. On or about 03.06.2011, the Accused-Appellant solicited
Rs.50,000/- from Mohamed Jesmi (PW01) and thereby
committed an offence punishable under Section 19(b) of the
Bribery act.
2. On the same transaction the Accused-Appellant solicited
Rs.50,000/- from Mohamed Jesmi and thereby committed an
offence punishable under Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act.
3. On the same day and during the same transaction the Accused-
Appellant accepted Rs.25,000/- from PW04 and thereby
3 | P a g e
committed an offence punishable under section 19(b) of the
Bribery Act.
4. On the same day and during the same transaction the Accused-
Appellant accepted Rs.25,000/- from PW04 and thereby
committed an offence punishable under Section 19(c) of the
Bribery Act.
5. On 17.06.2011 the Accused-Appellant accepted Rs.10,000/-
from PW01 and thereby committed an offence punishable under
section 19(b) of the Bribery Act.
6. On the same transaction the Accused-Appellant accepted the
Rs.10,000 /- from PW01 and thereby committed an offence
punishable under Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act.
7. On 03.06.2011 the Accused-Appellant accepted Rs.60,000/-
from PW01 and thereby committed an offence punishable under
section 19(b) of the Bribery Act.
8. On 03.06.2011 the Accused-Appellant accepted Rs.60,000/-
from PW01 and thereby committed an offence punishable under
Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act.
After the trial the Appellant was found guilty of 1st to 4th charges and he was
acquitted from the 5th to 8th charges. The Learned High Court Judge of
Colombo on 30/11/2023 has imposed the following sentences:
1. For every count a fine of Rs.5,000/- with a default sentence of 6
months simple imprisonment.
2. For every count 3 years rigorous imprisonment was imposed and
each sentence was to run concurrently.
4 | P a g e
3. Additionally, a fine of Rs.25000/- was imposed subject to a
default sentence of 06 months simple imprisonment.
Being aggrieved by the aforesaid conviction and sentence, the Appellant
preferred this appeal to this court.
The Learned Counsel for the Appellant informed this court that the Appellant
has given consent to argue this matter and he was present in court upon
being granted bail pending appeal.
On behalf of the Appellant the following Grounds of Appeal are raised.
1. The Learned High Court Judge had failed to consider material
contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and
thereby arrived at a wrong conclusion that the prosecution had proved
the charges beyond reasonable doubt.
2. The Learned High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the dock
statement of the Accused-Appellant, and thereby failed to adduce
proper reasons in rejecting the dock statement.
Background of the case.
In this case PW01 Mohamed Jesmi, had started a hotel business renting a
building from PW4, Mohamed Samath. On 03.06.2011, the Appellant who
was the Assistant to an Engineer of the Water Board had visited PW1’s hotel
and inspected the water supply to the hotel. After inspection, the Appellant
had informed PW1 that the water had been taken illegally to the said
building. Immediately, PW1 had informed PW4 about the incident and PW4
had admitted the allegation. The Appellant informed PW1 that Rs.500,000/-
would be payable to the Water Board by him. Upon hearing this, the
Appellant had solicited Rs.50,000/- to adjust the amount payable to the
Water Board. As per the request, Rs.25,000/- was paid to the Appellant by
5 | P a g e
PW4. On the same day the Appellant had provided the new estimate which
amounted to Rs.124,656/-. PW1 was asked to pay Rs. 60,000/- within a
week. The Appellant had then directed them to pay the balance of the new
estimate and the balance of the solicited amount Rs.25,000/- within two
weeks. According to PW1, he had given money to PW4, and PW4 had
informed after about two days that he had paid Rs. 60,000/- to the Water
Board.
When PW1 and PW4 were ready with the balance money, the Appellant had
informed that he would be coming to the hotel to collect the same. Having
felt suspicion regarding the transaction, PW4 had decided to complain to the
Bribery Commission.
After the complaint, upon the Appellant’s arrival to collect the money, PW1
had given Rs.70,000/- to him. At that time, the Bribery officials had arrested
him and recovered the money from the Appellant’s hand.
According to PW2, PS 31551 Liyanage, PW1 had informed that the Appellant
had requested Rs.60,000/- being the balance payment of the estimate and
Rs. 10,000/- from the balance solicited amount on the day of the raid. When
the Appellant collected the money, he had counted the money and put the
money into his trouser pocket. Upon seeing PW2 and PW3, the Appellant had
thrown the money to the second shelf of the showcase which was in the hotel.
As the Appellant refused to pick up the money from the shelf, PW3,
SI/Wimalaratne had picked up the same from the second shelf.
Although PW1 had testified that PW4 had told him that Rs.60,000/- was
paid to the Water Board, PW5, the Chief Engineer of the Water Board
confirmed that no money was received by the Water Board. PW5 further
confirmed that the estimate was prepared upon receiving correct information
from the Appellant.
Considering the first ground of appeal, the Appellant contends that the
Learned High Court Judge had failed to consider material contradictions in
6 | P a g e
the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and thereby arrived at a wrong
conclusion that the prosecution had proved the charges beyond reasonable
doubt.
The learned Counsel for the Appellant strenuously argued that although, the
complainant stated that he was supposed to pay Rs.25000/- and
Rs.64,656/- to the Appellant on the day of the arrest, in the complaint they
had said that they had to pay Rs.70,000/- only. Considering this
discrepancy, the Learned High Court Judge had acquitted the Appellant from
count numbers 5-8.
Further, the complainant had said that Rs.60,000/- was paid to the Water
Board through PW4 who was the owner of the hotel. Under cross
examination at page 240 of the brief, the complainant admitted that he did
not pay any money to the Water Board. PW5, the Engineer of the Water Board
stated that the Board had not received any money from the complainant or
any other person.
According to PW1, after receiving the money, the Appellant had the money
in his hand when PW2 and PW3 had apprehended him. The relevant portion
is re-produced below:

8 | P a g e
Although this is a glaring discrepancy between the evidence given by PW1,
PW2 and PW3, this has escaped the attention of the Learned High Court
Judge.
In Kalinga Padmatilaka v The Director General of Commission to
Investigate Allegation of Bribery or Corruption SC Appeal 99/2007
decided on 30.07.2009 the Supreme Court held that:
“It has to be stressed here that credibility of prosecution witnesses
should be subject to judicial evaluation in totality and not isolated
scrutiny by the Judge. When witnesses make inconsistent statements
in their evidence either at one stage or at 2 stages, the testimony of such
witnesses is unreliable and in the absence of special circumstances, no
conviction can be based on the testimony of such witnesses. On the
other hand, one cannot be unmindful of the proposition that Court cannot
mechanically reject the evidence of any witness”.
In Gurcharan Singh V. State of Haryana - Criminal Law Journal 1994 (2)
171 the Court held that:
“Where the material witnesses make inconsistent statements in their
evidence on material particulars, the evidence of such witnesses
becomes unreliable and unworthy of credence, thus making the
prosecution case highly doubtful.”
These contradictions would be of importance in view of the fact that the
Appellant had consistently taken the stance that no money was ever given to
him and that nothing was recovered from him.
9 | P a g e
Although the above mentioned inter se contradictions were not marked, it is
the duty of the Trial Judge to consider such evidence favourable to the
Accused with utmost care.
At one point the Court had severely warned PW1 to tell the truth.
During the cross examination, PW3 SI/Wimalaratna had stated that they
had recorded statements from several persons, however, the prosecution had
not served copies of the same even though they had requested for. Even the
Learned High Court Judge by his order dated 19.07.2019 had refused the
said application. This clearly shows that the Appellant had not been afforded
a fair trial.
Article 13(3) of the Constitution of Sri Lanka guarantees the right to a fair
trial; which ensures that every charged person has the right to be heard in
person or by a lawyer. It must be remembered at all times, that the “golden
thread” of criminal law emphasises on the presumption of innocence of an
Accused until his guilt is proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
In the Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 the court held that:
“It is fundamental that the burden of proof is on the prosecution.
Whether the evidence the prosecution relies on is direct or
circumstantial, the burden is the same. This burden is not altered by the
failure of the appellant to give evidence and explain the circumstances”.
In the case of Officer - In - Charge, Police Station Udu Dumbara Vs. U.G.
Sunil and Others (SC/APPEAL/27/2019), decided on 05.06.2024 it was
noted:
“It has been firmly established that, in a criminal case, that the charges
against the Accused should be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Proof
beyond a reasonable doubt generally means the Court must carefully
consider the entirety of admissible evidence to such scrutiny to see
10 | P a g e
whether the ingredients of the charges are proved. If the Court is not
satisfied the accused person must be acquitted.”
The case of Dietrich v The Queen [1992] HCA 57 established that the right
to a fair trial is an integral part of modern common law and due process.
In the second ground of appeal the Appellant contended that the learned
High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the dock statement of the Accused-
Appellant, and thereby failed to adduce proper reasons in rejecting the dock
statement.
A dock-statement, though considered as evidence, is subject to the infirmity
that it was not given under oath and thus cannot be subject to cross-
examination.
In Queen Vs. Buddharakkitha Thera and 2 Others 63 NLR 433, it had been
held that;
“the right of an accused person to make an unsworn statement from the
dock is recognized by our law. That right would be of no value unless such
a statement is treated as evidence on behalf of the accused subject
however to the infirmity which attaches to statements that are unsworn
and have not been tested by cross-examination.”
In Queen v. Kularatne 71 NLR 529 as follows;
“We are in respectful agreement, and are of the view that such a statement
must be looked upon as evidence subject to the infirmity that the accused
had deliberately refrained from giving sworn testimony, and the jury must
be so informed. But the jury must also be directed that,
11 | P a g e
(a) If they believe the unsworn statement, it must be acted upon,
(b) If it raised a reasonable doubt in their minds about the case for the
prosecution, the defense must succeed, and
(c) That it should not be used against another accused.”
In this case, the Learned High Court Judge had simply rejected the dock
statement without giving any reasons for the rejection. In his judgment, at

Credibility refers to a witness’ trustworthiness and reliability based on their
consistency, accuracy and veracity.
12 | P a g e
Credibility evidence would consist of evidence admitted in order to
strengthen or weaken the testimony of a witness or an accused. Such
evidence to impeach a witness can be submitted at any point from the time
the witness takes the stand. It is a standard rule that a witness would always
make their credibility vulnerable to attack whenever they testify. It should
be remembered that evidence that bolster’s a witness’s credibility would not
be admittable until the credibility of that witness has been impeached.
Similarly, there will no presumption of honesty among witnesses in a
criminal trial. As such, when testimony is given, the trier of fact must
determine whether such testimony is to be believed.
In the case of K. Padmathilaka alias Sergeant Elpitiya v. The Director
General of Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery and
Corruption [2010] BLR 67 the court held that:
“Credibility of prosecution witnesses should be subject to judicial
evaluation in totality and not isolated scrutiny by the judge. When witness
makes an inconsistent statement in their evidence either at one stage or
two stages, the testimony of such witness is unreliable……It is a cardinal
principle that unreliable evidence cannot be rendered credible, simply
because there is some corroboration material”.
In the case of Joy Devaraj v The State Of Kerala (2024) INSC 473 it was
held:
“The threshold for disbelieving a witness is not mere discrepancy or
inconsistency but material discrepancy and inconsistency, which
renders the account narrated by the witnesses so highly improbable that
the same may safely be discarded altogether from consideration.”
13 | P a g e
In this case, credibility of the prosecution witnesses has been clearly
impeached at very material points as dealt in the judgment. Further, the
Learned High Court Judge had misdirected himself in assessing the dock
statement of the Appellant. Therefore, I conclude that the appeal grounds
raised by the Appellant has merit. For the reasons stated above, I allow the
appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence imposed on the Appellant.
The Appellant is acquitted from all the charges.
